text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, poultry disease recognition should focus on detecting unusual flock-level changes early, while recognizing that similar symptoms occur across several diseases. Newcastle disease can spread rapidly, causing respiratory, digestive, or neurological signs (coughing, diarrhea, tremors, paralysis, twisted neck, circling, reduced/abnormal egg production, unusual deaths). Avian influenza can range from mild to severe with sudden death and high mortality depending on strain. Infectious bronchitis commonly causes coughing, sneezing, watery eyes, and reduced growth/egg production. Coccidiosis causes intestinal damage — reduced appetite, lethargy, poor growth, diarrhea, sometimes significant mortality. During the wet season (roughly May–October), watch for wet litter, mud, contaminated water, poor ventilation, and increased contact with wild birds; during the dry season (roughly November–April), heat stress, dehydration, and crowding around water sources create additional risk. Symptoms cannot reliably distinguish Newcastle disease from avian influenza — the chatbot should never tell a farmer a flock definitely has one of these based on description alone. Practical response: notice sudden changes in mortality, feed/water consumption, egg production, droppings, breathing, or neurological behavior; separate visibly sick birds where feasible; avoid unnecessary movement/mixing; escalate suspected severe outbreaks (especially sudden unexplained deaths or severe respiratory/neurological disease) to veterinary or animal-health authorities for investigation and testing. No specific chicken breed is assigned as predominant in Preah Vihear without reliable evidence — record the farmer's actual bird type.
